title: Git Lab: version control, taught
outcomes: Predict the state of the working tree, staging area, history and branch labels after any sequence of the taught commands.
Build focused commits, branch, merge, rebase and reset deliberately, choosing between alternatives and saying why.
Recover committed work after a bad reset or rebase, and say which losses Git cannot undo.
Repair a messy repository from a written plan and document it in a reproducible repair log.

lessons.title: Snapshots: working tree, staging area, commit
outcomes: Name the three places a file version can live: the working tree, the staging area (index) and a commit.
Predict exactly which version of a file a commit will hold, given a sequence of edits and adds.
Build focused commits by staging only the changes that belong together.
Read `git status`, `git diff` and `git diff --cached` to see which of the three places differ.
prerequisites: Can create and read text files and enter basic shell commands.

concept: A commit is a snapshot: a complete copy of every tracked file, frozen with a message and a link to the commit before it. It is not a list of edits.

Git keeps three copies of each tracked file. The working tree is what you edit. The staging area (also called the index) is the draft of your next snapshot. The last commit is the snapshot you already saved.

`git add file` copies the file's current contents from the working tree into the staging area. `git commit -m message` freezes the staging area into a new commit. Edits you make after `git add` stay in the working tree until you add again.
`git status` compares the three places. `git diff` shows working tree vs staging area. `git diff --cached` shows staging area vs last commit. If both are empty, all three copies agree.
Because you choose what to stage, one messy afternoon of edits can become several small, honest commits. That is what reviewers and your future self read.
assumptions: You are in the Git Lab's virtual shell. Nothing touches a real disk, network or account.

Commit ids here are short labels (c1, c2 …) given in creation order. Real Git hashes the commit: its snapshot, parent(s), author, committer, timestamps and message. Most repositories use 40 hex characters (SHA-1); SHA-256 repositories use 64. The same snapshot can have different commit ids.
The repository is the folder where you ran `git init` (here, /home).

Something is staged. Nothing tracked differs from what is staged. status.txt is still untracked.

Working tree vs staging area. plan.txt: the - line is the staged version, the + line is the working version. This lab also lists the untracked status.txt with an empty old side; real Git's plain `git diff` leaves untracked files out.
Stage everything in the repository: the new plan line and the untracked status.txt.
Staging area vs last commit: this is exactly what the next commit will change.

questions.prompt: note.txt said 'draft two' when you ran `git add`, and you then changed it to 'draft three'. You now run `git commit -m "Revise note"`. What does the new commit hold for note.txt?
choices: draft three
draft two
draft one
Nothing: the commit is refused because the file changed
why: The working tree says draft three, but a commit is built from the staging area, not the working tree.
Right: `git add` copied draft two into the staging area, and commit freezes the staging area.
draft one is in the previous commit c1; the staging area moved past it when you added.
Commit only needs a staged change that differs from the last commit. Later working-tree edits don't block it; they simply aren't included.

questions.prompt: `git diff` prints nothing, but `git diff --cached` shows a change to map.txt. What will `git commit -m "Update map"` do?
choices: Commit the map.txt change; working tree, staging area and the new commit then all agree
Refuse, because the working tree has no changes
Commit nothing, because diff was empty
Commit map.txt and also any untracked files
why: Right: empty `git diff` means working tree = staging area; the cached diff is exactly what the commit adds.
Commit compares the staging area with the last commit, not the working tree.
`git diff` without --cached only compares working tree and staging area.
Untracked files are never included until you add them.

misconceptions.claim: “git commit saves every file I changed.”
misconceptions.truth: Only staged changes go in. b.txt's edit is still only in the working tree, and status says so (Unstaged: yes). This is a feature: it is how you keep unrelated edits out of a commit.

misconceptions.claim: “Once a file is added, Git keeps tracking my edits automatically.”
misconceptions.truth: Tracking means Git compares the file; it does not stage new versions for you. Each new version has to be added again before a commit can include it.

realGit.here: Commit ids c1, c2 …
realGit.realGit: 40-character hashes such as 3f9a1c…; you can type a unique prefix.
realGit.note: Same idea: one id per snapshot.

realGit.here: `git status` prints Staged / Unstaged / Untracked lines
realGit.realGit: Longer output: 'Changes to be committed', 'Changes not staged for commit', 'Untracked files', with per-file names.
realGit.note: Read it the same way: three comparisons.

realGit.here: `git diff` prints the path and whole old/new text, and also lists untracked files
realGit.realGit: Unified diff with @@ hunks and line numbers; plain `git diff` ignores untracked files (use `git status` to see them).
realGit.note: Same pair of places compared for tracked files.

realGit.here: No author setup needed
realGit.realGit: Set `git config --global user.name` and `user.email` once before your first commit.

realGit.here: Whole-file staging only
realGit.realGit: `git add -p` stages part of a file; `git restore --staged file` unstages.
realGit.note: Unstaging appears here in the Reset lesson as `git reset --mixed`.

realGit.here: `git init` names the first branch main
realGit.realGit: With no configuration, current Git 2.x still defaults to master and prints a hint. Use `git init -b main` explicitly, or set `git config --global init.defaultBranch main` once.

lessons.title: Branches: movable labels on history
outcomes: Explain a branch as a named label that points at one commit and moves forward when you commit on it.
Say which branch HEAD is on and predict which commit a new commit's parent will be.
Predict how `git switch` changes the working tree, and why files 'vanish' and come back.
Start a branch from the right place, so unrelated work doesn't leak between branches.

concept: A branch is not a folder or a copy of your files. It is a name that points at one commit. Creating a branch costs nothing: no files are copied.
HEAD means 'the branch you are on'. When you commit, the new commit's parent is the commit your current branch points at, and only that branch label moves forward to the new commit.

`git switch name` moves HEAD to another branch and rewrites the tracked files in the working tree to match that branch's snapshot. A file that only exists on another branch disappears from the folder, but it is safe inside that branch's commit.
Untracked files belong to no branch. Switching leaves them where they are unless the target branch tracks the same path; real Git then refuses to overwrite the untracked file.
Where you stand when you create a branch matters: `git switch -c new` starts the new label at the current commit. Start from the wrong branch and the new branch quietly includes work it should not.
assumptions: In this lab you can switch only when no tracked file has uncommitted changes. Real Git is more permissive (see the Real Git table), but committing or undoing first is the safe habit in both.
There is no detached HEAD here: HEAD is always on a named branch.

walkthrough.title: A lighthouse branch and a pier branch

steps.narration: Make a new label lighthouse pointing at c1, the commit you are on. No files are copied, and you are still on main.
List the labels; the star marks HEAD.
HEAD moves to lighthouse. Both labels point at c1, so no files change.
Write a new file on the lighthouse branch.
Stage it.
c2's parent is c1. Only the current label, lighthouse, moves to c2; main stays at c1.
Back to main. Its snapshot c1 has no lamp.txt, so the file leaves the working tree. It is still safe in c2.
Create pier at main's commit c1 and switch to it in one step.
Work for the pier branch.
Stage it.
c3 also has parent c1. History has forked: lighthouse and pier have diverged from main.
lamp.txt returns and pier.txt leaves. Each branch shows its own snapshot; nothing was lost.

questions.prompt: You are on main with an uncommitted edit to map.txt. lighthouse holds a different committed version of map.txt. What happens when you run `git switch lighthouse`?
choices: It switches and your edit is lost
It refuses and changes nothing, so you can commit or undo first
It switches and commits your edit to lighthouse
It switches and your edit comes along
why: Git never silently throws away uncommitted work on a switch.
Right: lighthouse holds a different committed map.txt, so switching would overwrite the uncommitted edit. Git refuses and keeps main and the file unchanged.
Switching never makes a commit.
Real Git can carry edits when both branches hold the same version. Here lighthouse has different text, so the switch would overwrite the edit and is refused.

questions.prompt: main and docs both point at c4. You are on docs and commit c5. Then you run `git switch -c fix`. Where does fix point?
choices: c4, because branches start where main is
c5, the commit you are on
Nowhere until you commit on it
c4, because new branches start at the first commit
why: New branches start at HEAD, not at main.
Right: you were on docs at c5, so fix starts at c5 and includes that commit.
A branch always points at a commit; it starts at HEAD's commit.
Branches start at the current commit, not at the root.

misconceptions.truth: No new commit and no new files: just a second name for c1. Branches are cheap, so make one for every experiment.
On main the file was absent because main's snapshot doesn't contain it. Switching back restores it from c2.

misconceptions.claim: “My untracked notes belong to the branch I wrote them on.”
misconceptions.truth: A branch points at a commit, and commits only hold tracked files. Untracked files stay in the folder across switches unless the target branch tracks the same path: real Git refuses that switch to protect the file.

realGit.here: Any uncommitted tracked change blocks `git switch`
realGit.realGit: Switch succeeds and carries edits along if the target branch has the same version of those files; it refuses only if an edit would be overwritten. `git stash` can set edits aside.
realGit.note: The prediction now uses different committed file versions, so real Git and the lab both refuse.

realGit.here: No detached HEAD
realGit.realGit: `git switch --detach c1` (or checking out a commit id) puts HEAD on a commit with no branch; new commits there are easy to lose.
realGit.note: The Recovery lesson shows how to get lost commits back.

realGit.here: `git branch name` starts at the current commit
realGit.realGit: `git branch name <commit>` can start anywhere; `git branch -d name` deletes a label.

realGit.here: `git checkout` and `git switch` both switch
realGit.realGit: Same; `switch` is the newer, clearer command. `checkout` also restores files.

realGit.here: Untracked file collides with a tracked target path
realGit.realGit: `git switch` refuses: The following untracked working tree files would be overwritten by checkout. Move or preserve the untracked file before retrying.
realGit.note: Unlike --hard reset, switch protects this untracked content.

lessons.title: Merge: bringing lines of work together
outcomes: Tell a fast-forward merge from a merge commit by looking at the graph before you merge.
Predict which label moves when you merge, and in which direction to merge.
Predict when two branches conflict, and resolve a conflict by agreeing the shared file on the feature branch first.
Read a merge commit: two parents, a snapshot containing both lines of work.

concept: `git merge other` brings the work of other into the branch you are on. Only your current label moves; other stays where it was.
If your branch hasn't moved since other started, nothing needs combining: Git just slides your label forward to other's commit. That is a fast-forward and it creates no new commit.

If both branches have new commits, Git finds their common ancestor (the last commit both share) and compares each side with it. A file changed on only one side takes that side's version. The result is saved as a merge commit with two parents.

A conflict happens when the same file changed on both sides in different ways. Git cannot know which version you want. In real Git you edit the file to the final text and commit. In this lab the merge refuses and changes nothing, so you decide the shared file on one side first.
Direction matters. On main, `git merge feature` updates main. On feature, `git merge main` updates feature and leaves main untouched.
assumptions: This lab compares whole files. Real Git compares line by line, so edits to different lines of one file usually merge cleanly there. Here any differing edits to the same file count as a conflict.
Merges here need a clean working tree, and the merge commit message is always “Merge <branch>”.

steps.narration: main hasn't moved since summer branched off c1. Nothing to combine, so main slides forward to c2. No new commit.
Start winter at c2.
Meanwhile main changes the menu.
Stage it.
main moves to c3.
On winter (c2), the menu is still just soup.
winter changes a different file: the hours.
Stage it.
c4's parent is c2. main (c3) and winter (c4) have diverged from their common ancestor c2.
Go to the branch that should receive the work.

Compared with c2, main changed only menu.txt and winter changed only hours.txt. No overlap, so Git writes merge commit c5 with two parents, c3 and c4, holding both changes. winter's label stays at c4.
main's history now includes both lines of work.

questions.prompt: From the common ancestor (price 4), main changed price.txt to 5 and sale changed it to 3. On main you run `git merge sale`. What happens in this lab?
choices: main gets price 3 (the branch you merge in wins)
main keeps price 5 (your branch wins)
It stops with a conflict on price.txt; you must choose the final text
Git averages them to price 4
why: Neither side wins automatically. Both changed the same file differently.
Git won't silently drop the other side's change.
Right: same file, two different changes from the ancestor. You must decide the final text. Real Git also stops here, writes conflict markers into price.txt and waits for you.
Git never invents content.

questions.prompt: feature has 2 new commits and main has 0 new commits since feature started. On main you run `git merge feature`. How many new commits does the merge create?
choices: 0, it's a fast-forward
1 merge commit
2 copies of feature's commits
It refuses until main has a commit
why: Right: main's label just moves to feature's tip.
A merge commit needs new work on both sides.
Merge never copies commits; rebase does (next lesson).
Nothing needs combining, so there is nothing to refuse.

misconceptions.truth: main had no new commits, so the label just moved forward. A merge commit only appears when both sides have new work.

misconceptions.claim: “`git merge` direction doesn't matter: both branches end up the same.”
misconceptions.truth: Only the branch you are on moves. Here polish now contains main's work, but main still lacks polish's. To update main, switch to main first.

misconceptions.claim: “If both branches touch the same file, it's always a conflict.”
misconceptions.truth: Both sides made the same change, so there is nothing to choose between. Conflicts happen only when the two results differ. That is also how you resolve one in this lab: agree the file on one side first.

realGit.here: Same file changed differently on both sides → refuse, nothing changes
realGit.realGit: Git merges line by line. Overlapping lines stop the merge with <<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>> markers. You edit the file, then `git add` it and `git commit`; or `git merge --abort` to back out.
realGit.note: Resolution with markers is not practised in this lab.

realGit.here: Merge commit message is “Merge <branch>”
realGit.realGit: Default is “Merge branch '<branch>'” and opens an editor; `--no-edit` keeps the default.
realGit.note: The parity check maps one to the other.

realGit.here: Merge needs a clean working tree
realGit.realGit: Allowed if the merge doesn't touch your edited files, but a clean tree is the safe habit.

realGit.here: Fast-forward when possible
realGit.realGit: Same; `git merge --no-ff` forces a merge commit to record that a branch existed.

realGit.here: Lab conflict leaves files unchanged
realGit.realGit: A conflicting real merge writes <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers; git status reports unmerged paths and MERGE_HEAD records the unfinished merge. Resolve, git add and git commit, or git merge --abort to return to the pre-merge state.
realGit.note: Start with a clean working tree. You cannot switch branches mid-merge; run git merge --abort before the lab-style resolve-on-feature recipe.

referenceCard.recognise: Work on another branch is ready to join the branch you're on.
pitfalls: Expecting a merge commit after a fast-forward.
Resolving a conflict by discarding the other side's unrelated work.
referenceCard.model: merge = compare both sides with their common ancestor; one-sided changes combine; two-sided differences conflict

lessons.title: Rebase: replaying work on a new base
outcomes: Explain rebase as copying your branch's commits, in order, onto another commit, which produces new commits with new ids.
Use rebase then a fast-forward merge to land a feature with a straight-line history.
Predict what happens to the old commits, and why rebasing a branch someone else uses creates duplicates.
Choose between merge and rebase for a given situation and say why.

concept: On feature, `git rebase main` finds the commits feature has that main doesn't. It replays each one's change, in order, on top of main's tip, then moves feature's label to the last copy.
The copies are new commits: same message and same change, but a different parent, so a different id. The originals are not edited. They still exist, but no branch points at them any more.
After a rebase, feature sits directly on top of main, so `git merge feature` from main is a fast-forward and history stays a straight line. That is easier to read, bisect and review.

Merge keeps history exactly as it happened. Rebase rewrites your branch's history to look as if you started later. Rule of thumb: rebase your own unshared branch to tidy it; merge anything others have already built on.
Rebase compares files just as merge does, so a two-sided change to the same file still conflicts.
assumptions: This lab's rebase is meant for a simple feature branch whose own history is a straight line. It doesn't preserve merges inside the branch.
Each replayed commit applies its whole-file changes, so the conflict rule from the Merge lesson applies.

misconceptions.truth: It copies them. The old commit c2 is still in the graph (the lab dims it as unreachable). That's why a rebase can be undone, as the Recovery lesson shows.

misconceptions.claim: “Rebase avoids conflicts that merge would hit.”
misconceptions.truth: Same two-sided change, same conflict. Rebase only changes the shape of history, not whether two edits disagree.

realGit.here: Conflict → refuse, nothing changes

realGit.here: Rebased branches stay local
realGit.realGit: If you already pushed, the remote rejects the rewritten branch unless you `git push --force-with-lease`. Only do that on a branch only you use.

lessons.title: Reset: moving the branch, the staging area and the files
outcomes: State exactly which of the three places `--soft`, `--mixed` and `--hard` change.
Pick the reset mode that undoes a commit, unstages a file, or throws away edits, and no more than that.
Predict what a hard reset does to untracked files, and to the commits it moves away from.
Combine reset with add and commit to squash or split commits.

concept: `git reset <mode> <commit>` always moves your current branch label to that commit. The mode decides how much else follows.
--soft moves only the label. The staging area and the files keep the newer content, so the undone commit's changes sit there staged, ready to commit again.
--mixed (Git's default) moves the label and resets the staging area to match. Your files are untouched, but the changes are now unstaged.

--hard moves the label, the staging area and the tracked files. Uncommitted working-tree edits are discarded. Unrelated untracked files stay, but an untracked file or directory in the way of a tracked path in the target commit is overwritten or removed without warning.
Reset doesn't destroy the commits it moves away from. They stay in the graph with no label. The next lesson uses that to recover them.

In the lab, `HEAD~1` means 'the first parent of the commit I am on'. You can also use an id from `git log`: if c1 is the base before two newer commits, `git reset --soft c1` moves back to that base and keeps both changes staged, ready for one replacement commit. With no commit named, reset uses the commit you're on, which is how `git reset --mixed` unstages everything and `git reset --hard` throws away edits.
assumptions: The lab names commits as c1, c2 … or `HEAD~1`. Real Git also accepts branch names, `HEAD~2` (two first-parent steps) and `HEAD^` (first parent, same as HEAD^1). On a two-parent merge, HEAD~1 is the tip you merged into; HEAD^2 is the tip you merged in.
--mixed resets the whole staging area. Real Git can unstage a single file with `git restore --staged file`.

walkthrough.title: Three resets on an essay
setup: echo draft with intro and typo > essay.txt

steps.narration: --soft: main moves back from c3 to c2. The staging area and the files still hold c3's content, so the undone changes are staged.
--mixed on the current commit (c2): the staging area goes back to c2. The files keep the edits, now unstaged. junk.txt was never in c2, so it's untracked again.
--hard on c2: the tracked file essay.txt goes back to c2's text. junk.txt is untracked, so the reset leaves it alone.
main's history no longer shows “Rushed edit”...

...but c3 still exists in the graph with no label (the lab draws it dimmed). Tidy junk.txt by hand. Careful: rm permanently deletes an untracked file; Git cannot recover content it never saved. Here a copy survives in c3 only because you committed it earlier.

questions.prompt: notes.txt was never added. You run `git reset --hard HEAD~1`. What happens to code.txt and notes.txt?
choices: code.txt goes back to v1; notes.txt is deleted
code.txt goes back to v1; notes.txt is left alone
Both are left alone; only the branch moves
The reset refuses because notes.txt is untracked
why: The target commit does not track notes.txt, so it is unrelated to this reset and stays. An untracked file in the way of a tracked target path would be overwritten.
Right: tracked files match the target. Here notes.txt survives because the target does not track that path; colliding untracked files would be overwritten.
That's --soft.
A hard reset does not refuse to protect untracked content: it overwrites or removes anything in the way of a tracked target path. Here notes.txt is not in the way and stays.

questions.prompt: Your last commit had the right files but a bad message. Which reset lets you commit the exact same changes again with a new message in one command after it?
choices: git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1
No reset can help
why: Right: the changes stay staged, so `git commit -m "better"` recreates the commit.
After --mixed the changes are unstaged, so you must stage them again (and `commit -a` would miss any newly added file).
That throws the changes away.
--soft is exactly this. Real Git also offers `git commit --amend`.

misconceptions.claim: “`reset --soft HEAD~1` undoes the change in my file.”
misconceptions.truth: Only the label moved. The bad line is still in your file and staged. To throw the change away you need --hard.

misconceptions.claim: “Reset deletes the commits I reset past.”
misconceptions.truth: c2 is still there; no branch points at it any more. In real Git it stays recoverable for weeks via the reflog before cleanup.
--mixed only unstages. The edit is still in your file; `git add` puts it back.

realGit.here: `git reset --mixed` unstages everything
realGit.realGit: `git reset` (no flag) is --mixed; `git restore --staged file` unstages one file.

realGit.here: `git reset --hard` with no commit throws away tracked edits
realGit.realGit: Same; `git restore file` discards edits to one file.
realGit.note: Never-staged edits are permanently discarded. A staged-only file is lost in practice, though its blob may survive for git fsck --lost-found until garbage collection.

realGit.here: Unrelated untracked files survive; untracked content in the way does not
realGit.realGit: `git reset --hard` overwrites untracked content in the way of tracked target paths. For unrelated untracked files, `git clean -n` previews removal and `git clean -f` deletes them permanently; inspect the preview first.

realGit.here: Reset only your own unshared history
realGit.realGit: Resetting a pushed branch rewrites history others have, just like rebase. Use `git revert` to undo a shared commit with a new commit.
realGit.note: revert is not modelled in the lab. Reverting a merge needs a mainline parent: `git revert -m 1 <merge-id>` keeps parent 1 as the baseline; choose that parent deliberately.

referenceCard.recognise: You need to undo a commit, unstage, squash, split, or throw away edits.
commands: git reset --hard <c>: label + staging area + tracked files
HEAD~1 = first parent of the current commit; real Git HEAD^2 = second parent of a merge
pitfalls: Using --hard before git status and preserving edits: never-staged edits are gone; staged blobs are at best recoverable with fsck until GC.
Assuming untracked content is safe: --hard overwrites it when it is in the way of a tracked target path; unrelated untracked files stay.
`--hard` also removes a new file that was only staged: staging made it tracked, and the target commit doesn't have it.

lessons.title: Recovery: getting lost work back
outcomes: Explain why a commit that vanished from `git log` after a reset or rebase is usually still recoverable.
Recover an exact earlier commit, as opposed to retyping a copy, after a bad reset or an unwanted rebase.
Save a lost commit onto a new branch without moving the branch you're on.

Distinguish committed work (recoverable until GC), staged-only work (lost in practice, blob may survive until GC), and never-staged edits (unrecoverable); use a backup branch for commits before risky steps.

concept: `git log` only shows commits reachable from the branch you're on. A reset or rebase moves a label, and the commits it leaves behind drop out of the log. They aren't deleted.
To recover one, you need its id. In this lab the commit graph shows every commit and dims the unreachable ones. In real Git, `git reflog` lists every commit HEAD has pointed at, newest first.

Run `git status` first. Commit or stash edits you want to keep before any --hard reset (real Git: git stash push -u includes untracked files): it discards uncommitted working-tree edits and can overwrite untracked content in the way. `git reset --hard <id>` moves your current branch back onto that exact commit, the same snapshot with the same id. Retyping the change makes a new commit that only looks the same.

In real Git, save a lost commit with `git branch rescue <id>`: this creates a label without moving your current branch or touching your files, even with uncommitted edits. The lab only supports creating a branch at HEAD, so its fallback is `git switch -c rescue`, then `git reset --hard <id>`; use that fallback only after `git status` and preserving all edits, then switch back.

Git cannot recover working-tree content it never saved with add or commit. A staged-only new file removed by --hard is lost in practice: real Git may recover its blob with `git fsck --lost-found` until garbage collection prunes it, without its original filename. Do not rely on that. Commit first. `git branch backup` protects commits before risky operations, but does not save uncommitted edits.
assumptions: The lab has no reflog. Read ids from the commit graph, or from earlier `git log` output.
The lab never garbage-collects. Real Git eventually removes unreachable commits (by default after weeks), so recover soon.

questions.prompt: You rebased topic (its old commit was c2; the copy is c4) and regret it. Which command puts topic back exactly as it was before the rebase?
choices: git reset --hard HEAD~1
git reset --hard c2
git merge main
Nothing can: the rebase replaced c2
why: HEAD~1 is c4's parent, c3: that is main's tip, not your old work.
Right: c2 is still in the graph, and resetting topic onto it restores the pre-rebase branch exactly.
Merging main does nothing here: main is already an ancestor of the rebased topic. Git reports "Already up to date." and leaves HEAD unchanged; it does not undo the rebase.
Rebase copies; the original c2 was never removed.

questions.prompt: Which of these can you recover with Git alone?
choices: A commit your branch no longer points at after `reset --hard`
Edits you never staged, discarded by `reset --hard`
A file you created and never added, then deleted with rm
Text you typed and never saved to the file
why: Right: it's a commit, so it still exists unreachable; find its id and reset or branch to it.
Never committed, so no snapshot holds it.
Git never saw the file.
Git only knows what's in files, and only what you commit.

misconceptions.claim: “If `git log` doesn't show it, it's deleted.”
misconceptions.truth: The log only walks back from your branch. c2 was there all along.
The edit “1 and 2 and 3” was never committed, so no commit holds it, and no reset or reflog can bring it back. Commit (even as “WIP”) before anything risky.

misconceptions.claim: “A staged new file is safe from a hard reset.”
misconceptions.truth: Staging made summary.txt tracked, and the target commit does not have it, so --hard removes it. It is lost in practice; real Git may recover its blob with `git fsck --lost-found` until garbage collection prunes it, without its original filename. Commit first.

realGit.here: Read ids from the commit graph
realGit.realGit: `git reflog` lists where HEAD has been. After a reset, `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` goes back one step. A rebase writes one reflog entry per replayed commit, so HEAD@{1} is still the rebased copy: use the branch's own reflog (`git reset --hard topic@{1}`) or `ORIG_HEAD`, or read the reflog for the entry just before `rebase (start)`.
realGit.note: Checked in real Git (2.50): after a two-commit rebase, topic@{1} and ORIG_HEAD are the pre-rebase tip and HEAD@{1} is not. The reflog is local and isn't pushed.

realGit.here: Rescue without touching files
realGit.realGit: Use `git branch rescue <hash>` to preserve the commit without moving HEAD or touching uncommitted files. Switch to it later only after checking `git status` and preserving edits.

realGit.here: Unreachable commits stay forever
realGit.realGit: `git gc` prunes them after the reflog expires (default 90 days for reachable entries, 30 for unreachable).

realGit.here: Deleted tracked file → `git reset --hard` brings it back
realGit.realGit: `git restore file` copies the staged version back over your edit; `git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree file` returns both to the last commit.

referenceCard.recognise: Work vanished after reset, rebase or a wrong branch move.
commands: git status first; preserve edits before --hard (real Git: git stash push -u includes untracked files)
Find the id: commit graph (lab) / `git reflog` (real Git)
git reset --hard <id>: move this branch back onto it
Real Git: git branch rescue <id> saves it without moving HEAD or touching files
git branch backup: before anything risky
Lab-only rescue fallback: switch -c rescue, reset --hard <id>, switch back; only after preserving edits
pitfalls: Retyping instead of recovering the original commit.
Confusing a rebased copy with its original: compare parents.
Expecting to recover never-staged edits; a staged-only file is lost in practice (its blob may survive until GC).
referenceCard.model: Committed = recoverable until GC; staged-only = lost in practice, blob may survive until GC; never saved by Git = gone
